docs.title: Microsoft Azure Training
docs.text:
Welcome to the Microsoft Azure Training repository.

This course provides a practical, hands-on learning path for Microsoft Azure cloud administration, infrastructure engineering, security, automation, and DevOps practices.

The goal is to develop the skills required for roles such as:

  • Azure Administrator
  • Cloud Engineer
  • Infrastructure Engineer
  • DevOps Engineer
  • Cloud Solutions Architect

This repository documents the learning journey through practical labs, projects, automation, and real-world Azure deployments.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By completing this course you will learn how to:

  • Understand Microsoft Azure cloud concepts
  • Manage Azure subscriptions and resources
  • Configure Microsoft Entra ID
  • Implement Azure networking
  • Deploy and manage virtual machines
  • Configure Azure storage
  • Deploy applications using Azure services
  • Manage containers and Kubernetes
  • Implement monitoring and security
  • Automate Azure deployments
  • Use Infrastructure as Code
  • Manage cloud costs
  • Design secure and resilient cloud environments

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: Before starting this course you should have a basic understanding of:

docs.title: Operating Systems
docs.text:
Recommended knowledge:

  • Windows administration
  • Linux administration
  • Command line usage
  • File permissions
  • Services and processes

docs.title: Networking Fundamentals
docs.text:
You should understand:

  • IP addressing
  • Subnets
  • DNS
  • DHCP
  • Routing
  • Firewalls
  • Ports and protocols
  • TCP/IP concepts

Recommended protocols:

  • HTTP/HTTPS
  • SSH
  • RDP

docs.title: Virtualisation
docs.text:
Basic understanding of:

  • Virtual machines
  • Hypervisors
  • Virtual networking
  • Storage concepts

Examples:

  • VMware
  • Hyper-V
  • VirtualBox
  • KVM

docs.title: Scripting Knowledge
docs.text:
Helpful but not mandatory:

  • Bash scripting
  • PowerShell
  • Python basics
  • JSON/YAML syntax

docs.title: Cloud Fundamentals
docs.text:
Recommended knowledge:

  • Cloud computing concepts
  • IaaS
  • PaaS
  • SaaS
  • Public vs private cloud
  • Shared responsibility model

The free tier provides enough resources to complete many of the labs in this course.

docs.title: ADR-001: Replace k3s ServiceLB with MetalLB
docs.text:
Status: Accepted

Date: 19 July 2026

docs.title: Context
docs.text:
The initial k3s installation includes ServiceLB (Klipper LoadBalancer), which automatically exposes Kubernetes LoadBalancer services using the node's IP address.

While ServiceLB is suitable for lightweight clusters and development environments, it is specific to k3s and does not reflect the networking model commonly used in production Kubernetes environments.

As the objective of this project is to demonstrate transferable Kubernetes and platform engineering skills, a more production-oriented load-balancing solution was required.

docs.title: Decision
docs.text:
The built-in k3s ServiceLB will be disabled and replaced with MetalLB.

MetalLB provides a standards-based implementation of the Kubernetes LoadBalancer service type for bare-metal clusters by allocating IP addresses from a dedicated pool on the local network.

For this homelab, MetalLB will manage addresses within the following range:

192.168.2.220 - 192.168.2.230

docs.title: Rationale
docs.text:
MetalLB was selected because it:

  • Implements the standard Kubernetes LoadBalancer model.
  • Is widely adopted for bare-metal Kubernetes deployments.
  • Provides experience with IP address pools and Layer 2 advertisements.
  • Closely mirrors cloud networking concepts found in AWS, Azure and Google Cloud.
  • Demonstrates skills that are directly transferable to production Kubernetes environments.

docs.title: Benefits
docs.text:
• Cloud-like networking on bare-metal infrastructure.
  • Improved understanding of Kubernetes networking concepts.
  • Better separation between infrastructure and application services.
  • Enables future deployment of externally accessible services such as Grafana, Argo CD and custom applications.
  • Increases the professional value of the project for portfolio and CV purposes.

docs.title: Trade-offs
docs.text:
• Requires additional Kubernetes resources to operate.
  • Introduces management of IP address pools.
  • Adds a dependency on MetalLB components.

docs.title: Implementation
docs.text:
The implementation consists of:

  • Disabling the built-in k3s ServiceLB.
  • Installing MetalLB using Helm.
  • Creating an IP address pool for the local network.
  • Configuring Layer 2 advertisements.
  • Migrating LoadBalancer services to MetalLB-managed IP addresses.

docs.title: Outcome
docs.text:
Replacing ServiceLB with MetalLB aligns the homelab more closely with enterprise Kubernetes deployments while providing practical experience with networking concepts commonly used in production environments.

This decision supports the project's primary objective of demonstrating real-world Kubernetes platform engineering skills to prospective employers.

docs.title: Raspberry Pi: k3s fails with "failed to find memory cgroup (v2)"
Environment
docs.text: Component Details Hardware Raspberry Pi Operating System Debian 12 (Bookworm) Kubernetes Distribution k3s Architecture ARM64

docs.title: Issue
docs.text:
During the initial k3s installation, the service failed to start.

The installation completed successfully, but the Kubernetes service entered a restart loop.

Error message:

Error: failed to find memory cgroup (v2)

Systemd reported:

k3s.service: Main process exited, code=exited, status=1/FAILURE

docs.title: Investigation
docs.text:
The k3s logs showed that the installation progressed through:

  • Database initialisation
  • Bootstrap data generation
  • Kine datastore startup

before failing during resource controller validation.

Checking the Raspberry Pi boot configuration:

cat /boot/firmware/cmdline.txt

showed that Kubernetes-required memory cgroup parameters were missing.

docs.title: Root Cause
docs.text:
Kubernetes requires Linux cgroup controllers to manage resources such as:

  • CPU limits
  • Memory limits
  • Pod resource quotas

The Raspberry Pi Debian configuration did not have the memory cgroup controller enabled during boot.

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text:
Updated:

/boot/firmware/cmdline.txt

Added the following parameters to the existing single-line configuration:

cgroup_memory=1 cgroup_enable=memory

Rebooted the Raspberry Pi:

sudo reboot

Verified cgroup availability:

cat /proc/cgroups | grep memory

Restarted k3s:

sudo systemctl restart k3s

Validated the cluster:

kubectl get nodes

docs.title: Lessons Learned
docs.text:
• Kubernetes installations should validate host prerequisites before deployment.
  • Raspberry Pi Kubernetes environments require additional kernel configuration compared with standard server installations.

  • Automation scripts should include pre-flight checks for:

  • cgroup availability

  • swap configuration
  • kernel modules
  • network requirements

docs.title: Future Improvement
docs.text:
The k3s installation script will be enhanced to detect missing Kubernetes prerequisites before attempting installation.

Planned checks:

  • Verify memory cgroup support
  • Validate kernel modules
  • Confirm required sysctl settings
  • Provide actionable remediation instructions

Welcome to the Basic Linux Training course.

This module introduces the Linux operating system and provides the foundation knowledge required before starting Linux administration.

You will learn about:

  • What Linux is
  • How Linux works
  • Linux history
  • Linux distributions
  • Linux server environments
  • How to access Linux systems

  • How to access a Linux system
  • Basic Linux terminology

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Linux is one of the most widely used operating systems in the world.

It powers:

  • Web servers
  • Cloud platforms
  • Network devices
  • Supercomputers
  • Mobile devices
  • Embedded systems
  • Enterprise applications

This module introduces the Linux operating system, its history, common distributions, and the basic concepts required before beginning Linux administration.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this module, you should understand:

  • What Linux is
  • How Linux differs from other operating systems
  • The history of Linux
  • What Linux distributions are
  • The difference between Linux desktop and server environments
  • Common Linux terminology
  • How Linux is used in modern IT environments
  • How Linux systems are accessed

docs.title: What is Linux?
docs.text:
Linux is an open-source operating system based on the Linux kernel.

An operating system provides the interface between:

+----------------------+
|   Applications       |
+----------------------+
|   Operating System   |
+----------------------+
|   Hardware           |
+----------------------+

Linux manages:

  • CPU resources
  • Memory
  • Storage
  • Network interfaces
  • User accounts
  • Security controls
  • Running applications

docs.title: Kernel
docs.text:
The kernel is the core component of Linux.

It manages communication between software and hardware.

Examples:

  • CPU scheduling
  • Memory management
  • Device drivers
  • Network communication

The kernel is responsible for allowing applications to communicate with the underlying hardware.

Check your kernel version:

uname -r

Example output:

6.18.34+rpt-rpi-v8

docs.title: Linux History
docs.text:
Linux has its roots in earlier operating systems and open-source projects.

Understanding the history helps explain why Linux is designed the way it is today.

docs.title: UNIX
docs.text:
Linux was heavily influenced by UNIX.

UNIX was developed in the 1970s and introduced many concepts still used today:

  • Multi-user systems
  • File permissions
  • Command-line administration
  • Small tools working together

Many Linux concepts originated from UNIX design principles.

docs.title: GNU Project
docs.text:
The GNU Project began in 1983 with the goal of creating a free UNIX-like operating system.

Many Linux systems include GNU tools such as:

  • Bash
  • Core utilities
  • Compilers
  • System libraries

docs.title: Linux Kernel
docs.text:
In 1991, Linus Torvalds created the first Linux kernel.

The project grew rapidly because:

  • The source code was freely available
  • Developers worldwide contributed
  • Organisations adopted Linux

Today Linux is maintained by thousands of contributors and is used across many industries.

docs.title: What is a Linux Distribution?
docs.text:
A Linux distribution combines several components into a complete operating system.

A distribution normally includes:

  • Linux kernel
  • System tools
  • Package manager
  • Applications
  • Configuration tools

Examples:

Distribution Common Use Ubuntu Servers, cloud, desktop Debian Stable servers Rocky Linux Enterprise systems Fedora Development/testing Arch Linux Advanced users

Package manager:

Example:

docs.title: Linux Server vs Desktop
docs.text: Linux can be used in many different environments.

Linux desktops are used for:

  • Web browsing
  • Office applications
  • Development
  • Personal computing

Examples:

  • Fedora Workstation

docs.text:
Linux servers are commonly used for:

  • Websites
  • Databases
  • Cloud workloads
  • Virtualisation
  • Containers
  • Enterprise applications

Servers often:

  • Run continuously
  • Have no graphical interface
  • Are managed remotely
  • Support automation

Example:

Administrator

      |
      |
      v

Linux Server

+----------------+
| Applications   |
| Databases      |
| Services       |
+----------------+

docs.title: Accessing Linux Systems
docs.text:
Linux systems can be accessed in several different ways depending on where they are running.

Common access methods include:

  • Local console access
  • Remote SSH access
  • Virtual machine console access
  • Cloud provider console access

docs.title: Local Console Access
docs.text:
A local console provides direct access to a Linux system.

Examples:

  • Physical server
  • Raspberry Pi
  • Linux workstation

A user authenticates using:

  • Username
  • Password

After login, Linux provides access to a command-line environment called the shell.

Example:

james@linux-server:~$

docs.title: Remote Access Using SSH
docs.text:
Linux servers are commonly managed remotely using SSH.

SSH means:

Secure Shell

SSH provides an encrypted connection between an administrator and a Linux system.

Example:

ssh username@hostname

Example:

ssh james@server01

SSH is widely used for:

  • Cloud servers
  • Enterprise servers
  • Remote administration

SSH administration will be covered in more detail in later modules.

docs.title: Virtual Machine and Cloud Access
docs.text:
Linux systems may also be accessed through:

  • Virtual machine consoles
  • Cloud provider management consoles
  • Remote management platforms

Examples:

  • AWS virtual machines
  • Microsoft Azure virtual machines
  • VMware environments

docs.title: Module 01 - Command Line Fundamentals
docs.text:
Estimated time: 60–90 minutes

Prerequisites: - Module 00 – Introduction to Linux

Difficulty: Beginner

Hands-on exercises: Yes

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The Linux command line is one of the most powerful tools available to a system administrator. While many operating systems provide graphical interfaces, Linux administration is primarily performed from the command line.

Learning the command line allows you to:

  • Work efficiently
  • Manage remote servers
  • Troubleshoot systems
  • Automate repetitive tasks
  • Manage thousands of files quickly
  • Perform administration without a graphical interface

This module introduces the Linux shell, explains how commands are structured, and teaches you how to move around the Linux filesystem confidently.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • Explain what the Linux shell is.
  • Understand the Linux command prompt.
  • Recognise the structure of a Linux command.
  • Display your current working directory.
  • Navigate around the filesystem.
  • List files and directories using different options.

docs.title: What is the Linux Shell?
docs.text:
The shell is a program that accepts commands from the user and passes them to the Linux kernel for execution.

Think of it as an interpreter between you and the operating system.

+---------------------+
|      User           |
+---------------------+
          |
          v
+---------------------+
|      Shell          |
|      (Bash)         |
+---------------------+
          |
          v
+---------------------+
|   Linux Kernel      |
+---------------------+
          |
          v
+---------------------+
|     Hardware        |
+---------------------+

The shell performs many useful functions including:

  • Running programs
  • Managing files
  • Launching applications
  • Executing scripts
  • Redirecting output
  • Automating repetitive tasks

The most common shell is Bash (Bourne Again SHell), although others exist such as:

  • Zsh
  • Fish
  • Korn Shell (ksh)
  • C Shell (csh)

To see which shell you are using, run:

echo $SHELL

Example output:

/bin/bash

docs.title: Understanding the Command Prompt
docs.text:
When you log into a Linux system you will normally see something similar to:

james@k3s-node-01:~$

This is known as the command prompt.

Let's break it down.

james @ k3s-node-01 : ~ $
│         │           │
│         │           └── Current directory
│         └────────────── Hostname
└──────────────────────── Username

The final character is important:

$

indicates a standard user.

Whereas:

#

indicates the root user.

Always check your prompt before running administrative commands.

docs.title: The Current Working Directory
docs.text:
Linux always keeps track of where you are in the filesystem.

This location is called the Current Working Directory (CWD).

To display it, use:

pwd

Example:

/home/james

If you are in another directory:

/etc

then:

pwd

returns:

/etc

Knowing your current location is important because many commands work relative to your current directory.

docs.title: Listing Files and Directories
docs.text:
The ls command displays the contents of a directory.

Basic usage:

ls

Example output:

Documents
Downloads
Pictures
projects

docs.title: Long Listing
docs.text:
To display more information:

ls -l

Example:

drwxr-xr-x 2 james users 4096 Jul 18 Documents
-rw-r--r-- 1 james users  245 Jul 20 notes.txt

This shows:

  • File permissions
  • Number of links
  • Owner
  • Group
  • File size
  • Date modified
  • File name

docs.title: Show Hidden Files
docs.text:
Files beginning with a full stop (.) are hidden by default.

Display them with:

ls -a

Example:

.
..
.bashrc
.profile
Documents
Downloads

docs.title: Human Readable Sizes
docs.text:
ls -lh

Example:

-rw-r--r-- 1 james users 2.4K notes.txt

Instead of displaying file sizes in bytes, -h shows them in a human-readable format such as KB, MB or GB.

docs.title: Navigating the Filesystem
docs.text:
Use the cd command to change directories.

Move to your home directory:

cd

or

cd ~

Move to another directory:

cd /etc

Check where you are:

pwd

Example:

/etc

docs.title: Moving Up One Directory
docs.text:
Use:

cd ..

Example:

If you are in:

/home/james/projects

running:

cd ..

takes you to:

/home/james

docs.title: Returning to the Previous Directory
docs.text:
Use:

cd -

Example:

/home/james

↓

cd /etc

↓

cd -

returns you to:

/home/james

docs.title: Going to the Root Directory
docs.text:
To move to the top of the Linux filesystem:

cd /

Verify your location:

pwd

Output:

/

docs.title: Absolute vs Relative Paths
docs.text: Linux understands two types of paths.

docs.title: Absolute Path
docs.text:
An absolute path always starts at the root directory (/).

Example:

/home/james/projects/basic-linux-training

No matter where you are currently located, this path always points to the same location.

docs.title: Relative Path
docs.text:
A relative path starts from your current location.

For example, if your current directory is:

/home/james

then:

cd projects

works because projects exists beneath your current directory.

docs.title: Visual Example
docs.text:
/

├── home
│   └── james
│       └── projects
│           └── basic-linux-training
│
├── etc
├── var
└── usr

If you are in:

/home/james

then:

cd projects/basic-linux-training

is a relative path.

Whereas:

cd /home/james/projects/basic-linux-training

is an absolute path.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
✔ Check your current location with pwd before making changes.

✔ Use ls -l when you need detailed file information.

✔ Prefer absolute paths when writing scripts.

✔ Use cd ~ to quickly return to your home directory.

✔ Be aware of whether you are a standard user ($) or the root user (#).

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this lesson you learned:

  • What the Linux shell is.
  • How the command prompt is structured.
  • How commands are entered.
  • How to identify your current directory.
  • How to navigate the filesystem.
  • The difference between absolute and relative paths.

In Part 2, you will learn how to create, copy, move and delete files and directories safely.

docs.title: Lesson 02 - Working with Files and Directories
docs.text:
Estimated time: 45–60 minutes

Difficulty: Beginner

Prerequisites: - Module 00 - Introduction to Linux - Lesson 01 - The Linux Shell and Navigation

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Now that you understand how to navigate the Linux filesystem, the next step is learning how to create, copy, move and remove files and directories.

These commands are used every day by Linux administrators and form the foundation of working with Linux systems.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • Create directories
  • Create empty files
  • Copy files and directories
  • Move and rename files
  • Remove files and directories safely
  • Use wildcards
  • Understand common command-line shortcuts

docs.title: Creating Directories
docs.text: The mkdir command creates new directories.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
mkdir directory_name

Example:

mkdir training

Verify the directory exists:

ls

Example output:

training

docs.title: Creating Multiple Directories
docs.text:
Multiple directories can be created in a single command.

Example:

mkdir docs scripts backups

Result:

docs
scripts
backups

docs.title: Creating Nested Directories
docs.text:
Normally Linux requires parent directories to already exist.

The -p option creates the complete directory structure.

Example:

mkdir -p projects/linux/module01

This creates:

projects
└── linux
    └── module01

docs.title: Creating Files
docs.text:
Linux uses the touch command to create empty files.

Example:

touch notes.txt

Verify:

ls

Output:

notes.txt

Multiple files can be created at once:

touch file1.txt file2.txt file3.txt

docs.title: Copying Files
docs.text: The cp command copies files.

docs.title: Syntax
docs.text:
cp source destination

Example:

cp notes.txt backup.txt

Result:

notes.txt
backup.txt

The original file remains unchanged.

docs.title: Copying Directories
docs.text:
Directories require the recursive option.

Example:

cp -r projects backup

The -r option means:

recursive

This copies the directory and everything inside it.

docs.title: Moving Files
docs.text:
The mv command moves files and directories.

Example:

mv notes.txt Documents/

The file is moved into the Documents directory.

docs.title: Renaming Files
docs.text:
The mv command is also used to rename files.

Example:

mv notes.txt lesson-notes.txt

The file has now been renamed.

docs.title: Removing Files
docs.text:
Files are removed using the rm command.

Example:

rm backup.txt

Once deleted, the file cannot normally be recovered.

Always check the filename before pressing Enter.

docs.title: Removing Directories
docs.text:
Empty directories can be removed using:

rmdir directory_name

Example:

rmdir training

docs.title: Removing Directories and Contents
docs.text:
To remove a directory and everything inside it:

rm -r directory_name

Example:

rm -r old-project

Be careful when using recursive deletion.

docs.title: The Dangerous Command
docs.text:
A very powerful command is:

rm -rf

The options mean:

Option Meaning -r Recursive -f Force

Example:

rm -rf test-directory

This removes the directory and contents without asking for confirmation.

⚠️ Never run a command unless you understand exactly what it will do.

docs.title: Using Wildcards
docs.text:
Wildcards allow commands to work with multiple files.

The most common wildcard is:

*

which means "match anything".

docs.title: Example - Delete All Text Files
docs.text:
rm *.txt

This removes all files ending with:

.txt

docs.title: Example - List Log Files
docs.text:
ls *.log

Displays files ending with:

.log

docs.title: Useful Keyboard Shortcuts
docs.text: Shortcut Description ↑ Previous command ↓ Next command Tab Auto-complete command or filename Ctrl + C Cancel current command Ctrl + L Clear terminal Ctrl + D Logout / end shell

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
✔ Check your location with:

pwd

before making changes.

✔ Use:

ls

before deleting files.

✔ Create backups before modifying important files.

✔ Avoid using:

rm -rf

unless you are completely certain.

✔ Use meaningful filenames.

✔ Keep files organised into directories.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Linux administrators spend a large amount of time reading configuration files, reviewing logs, and finding information about commands.

Unlike graphical operating systems, Linux provides powerful command-line tools for viewing and searching information quickly.

This lesson introduces the tools required to:

  • View file contents
  • Read large files
  • Monitor changing files
  • Find command documentation
  • Understand command options
  • Use command history

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • Display the contents of files
  • Read large text files safely
  • View the beginning and end of files
  • Monitor log files
  • Use Linux manual pages
  • Find help for commands
  • Review previously executed commands

docs.title: Creating Test Files
docs.text:
Before learning how to view files, create some example files.

Create a directory:

mkdir file-demo

Move into it:

cd file-demo

Create a file:

touch example.txt

Add some content:

echo "Linux command line training" > example.txt

Check the file exists:

ls

docs.title: The cat Command
docs.text:
The simplest way to display a file is using:

cat filename

Example:

cat example.txt

Output:

Linux command line training

cat is useful for small files.

docs.title: Viewing Line Numbers
docs.text:
Use:

cat -n filename

Example:

cat -n example.txt

Output:

1  Linux command line training

Line numbers are useful when troubleshooting configuration files.

docs.title: Reading Large Files
docs.text:
Large files can contain thousands of lines.

Examples:

  • Log files
  • Application configuration files
  • System reports

Using cat on very large files can make the terminal difficult to use.

For large files, use:

less

docs.title: The less Command
docs.text:
Example:

less /var/log/syslog

less allows you to scroll through files.

Useful keys:

Key Action Space Next page b Previous page ↑ Move up ↓ Move down / Search q Quit

Example search:

/error

finds occurrences of the word:

error

docs.title: Viewing the Beginning of Files
docs.text:
The head command displays the first lines of a file.

Example:

head example.txt

By default it shows the first 10 lines.

To show a specific number:

head -20 example.txt

Displays the first 20 lines.

docs.title: Viewing the End of Files
docs.text:
The tail command displays the last lines of a file.

Example:

tail example.txt

Useful for checking recent log entries.

Example:

tail /var/log/syslog

docs.title: Monitoring Log Files
docs.text:
Linux systems generate many log files.

Examples:

/var/log/syslog
/var/log/auth.log

To watch a log file as it changes:

tail -f /var/log/syslog

The -f option means:

follow

The terminal will continue displaying new entries.

Exit with:

Ctrl + C

docs.title: Getting Help in Linux
docs.text: Linux has several built-in ways to find help.

docs.title: The man Command
docs.text:
man displays the manual page for a command.

Example:

man ls

Output includes:

  • Command description
  • Available options
  • Examples
  • Related commands

docs.title: Searching Manual Pages
docs.text:
Example:

man -k password

Searches available manual pages containing:

password

docs.title: Command Help Options
docs.text:
Many commands provide their own help.

Example:

ls --help

Output:

Usage:
 ls [OPTION]... [FILE]...

Common help options:

--help
-h
-help

docs.title: Finding Command Locations
docs.text:
The which command shows where a command is installed.

Example:

which ls

Output:

/usr/bin/ls

docs.title: Understanding Commands
docs.text:

docs.text:
Linux stores previously executed commands.

history

Example:

docs.text:
Use the up arrow:

↑

to cycle through previous commands.

docs.title: Searching History
docs.text:
Press:

Ctrl + R

Then type part of a previous command.

Example:

ssh

Linux will search your command history.

docs.title: Combining Commands
docs.text:
Linux commands can be combined using pipes.

A pipe:

|

passes the output of one command into another.

Example:

ls /etc | less

This sends the output of ls into less.

Useful when commands produce a lot of output.

Ctrl + R

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Understanding how Linux organises files and controls access is a fundamental skill for every Linux administrator.

In this module you will learn how the Linux filesystem is structured, how file ownership and permissions work, and how to locate files efficiently. These skills are essential for managing systems securely and troubleshooting everyday administration tasks.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this module you will be able to:

  • Describe the Linux filesystem hierarchy.
  • Identify the purpose of common system directories.
  • Understand file ownership and group ownership.
  • Read and interpret Linux file permissions.
  • Modify permissions using chmod.
  • Change ownership using chown.
  • Locate files using common search tools.
  • Create and use symbolic links.

docs.title: Lesson 01 - Linux Filesystem Hierarchy
docs.text:
Estimated time: 45–60 minutes

Module: Module 02 – Linux Filesystem Administration

Prerequisites: - Module 00 – Introduction to Linux - Module 01 – Command Line Fundamentals

Difficulty: Beginner

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
One of the biggest differences between Linux and Windows is how files are organised.

Windows separates storage into multiple drives such as C:, D:, and E:. Linux, however, presents everything through a single directory tree that begins at the root directory (/).

Understanding where Linux stores configuration files, applications, logs and user data is an essential skill for any Linux administrator. Most Linux distributions follow a common layout known as the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS), making it easier to work across different systems.

In this lesson, you will explore the Linux directory structure and learn the purpose of the most important directories.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • Explain the Linux filesystem hierarchy.
  • Describe the purpose of the root directory.
  • Identify the function of common system directories.
  • Locate configuration files, applications and logs.
  • Navigate the filesystem confidently.
  • Apply best practices when working with the Linux filesystem.

docs.title: What is a Filesystem?
docs.text:
A filesystem defines how an operating system stores and organises data.

Every file, directory and device in Linux exists somewhere within a single directory tree.

Unlike Windows:

C:\
D:\
E:\

Linux starts from one location:

/

This is known as the root directory.

Everything on the system is connected beneath it.

docs.title: The Linux Filesystem Hierarchy
docs.text:
The Linux directory structure resembles an upside-down tree.

/
├── bin
├── boot
├── dev
├── etc
├── home
├── media
├── mnt
├── opt
├── proc
├── root
├── run
├── sbin
├── srv
├── sys
├── tmp
├── usr
└── var

Every directory has a specific purpose.

This consistency allows administrators to work confidently across different Linux distributions.

docs.title: Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS)
docs.text:
Most Linux distributions follow the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS).

The standard defines where different types of files should be stored.

For example:

Type of Data Typical Location User files /home Configuration files /etc System logs /var/log Installed applications /usr Temporary files /tmp Device files /dev

Following this standard makes Linux systems easier to understand, maintain and troubleshoot.

docs.title: Exploring the Root Directory
docs.text:
To display the contents of the root directory, run:

ls /

Example output:

bin
boot
dev
etc
home
media
mnt
opt
proc
root
run
sbin
srv
sys
tmp
usr
var

docs.title: /home
docs.text:
The /home directory stores personal files for normal users.

Example:

/home/james
/home/alice
/home/training

Each user has their own home directory.

To display your home directory:

echo $HOME

or

cd
pwd

docs.title: /root
docs.text:
This is the home directory of the root user.

Do not confuse:

/

with

/root

The first is the root of the filesystem.

The second is root's personal home directory.

docs.title: /etc
docs.text:
This directory contains system configuration files.

Examples include:

/etc/hostname
/etc/passwd
/etc/group
/etc/ssh/
/etc/systemd/

View the directory:

ls /etc

Administrators frequently work in /etc.

docs.title: /var
docs.text:
Variable data is stored here.

Examples include:

  • System logs
  • Databases
  • Print queues
  • Mail queues
  • Web server content

To view system logs:

ls /var/log

Many troubleshooting tasks begin in /var/log.

docs.title: /usr
docs.text:
This directory contains installed software and shared resources.

Common locations include:

/usr/bin
/usr/lib
/usr/share

Most applications installed using the package manager are stored beneath /usr.

docs.title: /bin
docs.text:
Contains essential user commands required for the operating system.

Examples:

ls
cp
mv
cat
bash

These commands are available even during system recovery.

docs.title: /sbin
docs.text:
Contains essential system administration commands.

Examples:

fsck
reboot
shutdown
ip

Many commands require administrative privileges.

docs.title: /tmp
docs.text:
Temporary files are stored here.

Applications use this location to hold temporary data while running.

Many Linux systems automatically clean this directory during boot.

docs.title: /boot
docs.text:
Contains files required to start Linux.

Examples include:

  • Linux kernel
  • Initial RAM filesystem (initramfs)
  • Boot loader configuration

docs.title: /dev
docs.text:
Linux treats hardware devices as files.

Examples:

/dev/sda
/dev/null
/dev/tty

Administrators rarely modify these directly, but they are important when managing disks and hardware.

docs.title: /proc
docs.text:
The /proc directory is a virtual filesystem.

It provides information about the running kernel and system processes.

Example:

cat /proc/cpuinfo

View memory information:

cat /proc/meminfo

No actual files are stored here—they are generated by the kernel.

docs.title: /sys
docs.text:
Another virtual filesystem.

Provides information about hardware devices and the Linux kernel.

It is commonly used by advanced administration tools.

docs.title: /opt
docs.text:
Used for optional or third-party software.

For example:

/opt/google
/opt/custom-application

Many commercial applications install here.

docs.title: Exploring the Filesystem
docs.text:
Useful commands include:

Display your current location:

pwd

Move to the root directory:

cd /

List directory contents:

ls

Detailed listing:

ls -l

Classify file types:

ls -F

If installed, display the directory tree:

tree /

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
✔ Store personal files inside your home directory.

✔ Avoid modifying files in /etc unless required.

✔ Learn where log files are stored.

✔ Never delete files from system directories without understanding their purpose.

✔ Use sudo carefully when working outside your home directory.

docs.title: Task 1 – Explore the Root Directory
docs.text:
Run:

ls /

Record five directories you recognise.

docs.title: Task 2 – Identify Your Home Directory
docs.text:
Run:

echo $HOME

Then:

pwd

Do they match?

docs.title: Task 3 – Explore System Configuration
docs.text:
Navigate to:

cd /etc

List the contents:

ls

Can you identify:

  • passwd
  • hostname
  • ssh

docs.title: Task 4 – View System Logs
docs.text:
Navigate to:

cd /var/log

List the contents:

ls

How many log files can you identify?

docs.title: Task 5 – Explore Installed Programs
docs.text:
Navigate to:

cd /usr/bin

Count the number of files:

ls | wc -l

Notice how many applications are available on a standard Linux installation.

docs.title: Knowledge Check
docs.text:
1. What is the top-level directory in Linux called?

  2. Which directory stores user home folders?

  3. Where are most system configuration files stored?

  4. Which directory contains system log files?

  5. What is the purpose of /tmp?

  6. Why is /proc described as a virtual filesystem?

  7. Which directory is commonly used for optional third-party software?

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this lesson you learned:

  • Linux uses a single directory tree beginning at the root directory (/).
  • Most Linux distributions follow the Filesystem Hierarchy Standard (FHS).
  • Configuration files are stored in /etc.
  • User data is stored in /home.
  • System logs are stored in /var/log.
  • Applications are commonly installed beneath /usr.
  • Temporary files are stored in /tmp.
  • Understanding the filesystem hierarchy is essential for effective Linux administration and troubleshooting.

docs.text: In Lesson 02 – File Permissions and Ownership, you will learn how Linux controls access to files and directories using users, groups and permissions.

docs.title: Lesson 02 - File Permissions and Ownership
docs.text:
Estimated time: 60–75 minutes

Module: Module 02 – Linux Filesystem Administration

Prerequisites: - Module 00 – Introduction to Linux - Module 01 – Command Line Fundamentals - Lesson 01 – Linux Filesystem Hierarchy

Difficulty: Beginner to Intermediate

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Linux is a multi-user operating system, which means multiple users can access the same system at the same time. To keep the system secure, Linux uses a permissions model that controls who can read, modify, or execute files and directories.

Every file and directory has an owner, belongs to a group, and has a set of permissions that determine what actions can be performed.

Understanding file permissions is essential for managing Linux systems, securing sensitive information, and troubleshooting access issues.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • Explain Linux ownership and permissions.
  • Identify the owner and group of a file.
  • Interpret the output of ls -l.
  • Understand read, write and execute permissions.
  • Modify permissions using chmod.
  • Change ownership using chown.
  • Change group ownership using chgrp.
  • Apply permission changes safely using best practices.

docs.title: Linux Ownership
docs.text:
Every file and directory has:

  • An owner (the user who owns the file)
  • A group (a collection of users)
  • A set of permissions

Display a long listing:

ls -l

Example output:

-rw-r--r-- 1 james developers 245 Jul 22 notes.txt

Breaking it down:

-rw-r--r-- 1 james developers 245 Jul 22 notes.txt
│─────────│ │     │
│         │ │     └── Group
│         │ └──────── Owner
│         └────────── Permissions

docs.title: Understanding Permissions
docs.text:
The first column represents the file type and permissions.

-rw-r--r--

Split into sections:

- rw- r-- r--
│ │   │   │
│ │   │   └── Others
│ │   └────── Group
│ └────────── Owner
└──────────── File type

docs.title: File Types
docs.text:
The first character identifies the file type.

Symbol Type - Regular file d Directory l Symbolic link c Character device b Block device

Example:

drwxr-xr-x

The d indicates a directory.

docs.title: Permission Types
docs.text:
There are three basic permissions.

Symbol Meaning r Read w Write x Execute

docs.title: Read (r)
docs.text:
Allows a file to be viewed.

Example:

cat notes.txt

docs.title: Write (w)
docs.text:
Allows the file to be modified.

Examples include:

  • Editing
  • Saving
  • Deleting (depending on directory permissions)

docs.title: Execute (x)
docs.text:
Allows a file to be run as a program or script.

Example:

./backup.sh

docs.title: Permission Groups
docs.text:
Permissions are applied to three groups.

Group Description Owner User who owns the file Group Members of the assigned group Others Everyone else

Example:

-rwxr-x---

Owner:

rwx

Group:

r-x

Others:

---

docs.title: Numeric Permissions
docs.text:
Permissions can also be represented using numbers.

Permission Value Read 4 Write 2 Execute 1

Examples:

Number Meaning 7 rwx 6 rw- 5 r-x 4 r-- 0 ---

Common combinations:

Numeric Symbolic 755 rwxr-xr-x 644 rw-r--r-- 700 rwx------ 600 rw-------

docs.title: Changing Permissions with chmod
docs.text:
Symbolic example:

chmod u+x backup.sh

Adds execute permission for the owner.

Remove write permission:

chmod g-w notes.txt

Numeric example:

chmod 644 notes.txt

Make a script executable:

chmod 755 backup.sh

docs.title: Changing Ownership
docs.text:
Display ownership:

ls -l

Change owner:

sudo chown james notes.txt

Change owner and group:

sudo chown james:developers notes.txt

docs.title: Changing Group Ownership
docs.text:
Use:

sudo chgrp developers notes.txt

Verify:

ls -l

docs.title: Directory Permissions
docs.text:
Permissions behave slightly differently on directories.

Permission Effect Read List contents Write Create, delete or rename files Execute Enter the directory using cd

Example:

chmod 755 projects

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
✔ Give users only the permissions they need.

✔ Avoid using 777.

✔ Use groups instead of assigning permissions to individual users wherever possible.

✔ Verify changes using ls -l.

✔ Use sudo only when necessary.

✔ Be especially careful when changing permissions in /etc, /usr or /var.

docs.title: Task 1 – View Permissions
docs.text:
Run:

ls -l

Identify:

  • Owner
  • Group
  • Permission string

docs.title: Task 2 – Create a File
docs.text:
touch training.txt
ls -l

Record its permissions.

docs.title: Task 3 – Make a Script Executable
docs.text:
Create a script:

touch backup.sh

Add execute permission:

chmod +x backup.sh

Verify:

ls -l backup.sh

docs.title: Task 4 – Change Numeric Permissions
docs.text:
Set:

chmod 644 training.txt

Then:

chmod 600 training.txt

Observe the changes.

docs.title: Task 5 – Change Group Ownership
docs.text:
If permitted:

sudo chgrp developers training.txt

Verify using:

ls -l

docs.title: Knowledge Check
docs.text:
1. What does the first character in ls -l output represent?

  2. What do the letters r, w and x mean?

  3. Which command changes file permissions?

  4. Which command changes file ownership?

  5. What numeric permission corresponds to rwxr-xr-x?

  6. Why should 777 permissions generally be avoided?

  7. Why are groups useful when managing permissions?

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this lesson you learned:

  • Every file has an owner and a group.
  • Linux permissions control access to files and directories.
  • Permissions are represented symbolically and numerically.
  • chmod changes permissions.
  • chown changes ownership.
  • chgrp changes group ownership.
  • Correct permissions are essential for both security and system administration.

docs.title: Lesson 03 - Finding Files and Links
docs.text:
Estimated time: 60–75 minutes

Module: Module 02 – Linux Filesystem Administration

Prerequisites: - Module 00 – Introduction to Linux - Module 01 – Command Line Fundamentals - Lesson 01 – Linux Filesystem Hierarchy - Lesson 02 – File Permissions and Ownership

Difficulty: Beginner to Intermediate

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
As Linux systems grow, they can contain thousands or even millions of files. System administrators need efficient ways to locate files, identify commands, and create links between files and directories.

In this lesson, you will learn how to search for files using a variety of tools, understand the differences between them, and use hard and symbolic links effectively.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • Find files using the find command.
  • Locate files quickly using locate.
  • Identify where commands are stored.
  • Understand hidden files.
  • Explain the difference between hard and symbolic links.
  • Create and remove links safely.

docs.title: Finding Files with find
docs.text:
The find command searches the filesystem in real time.

Basic syntax:

find <location> <criteria>

Search for a file by name:

find /home -name "notes.txt"

Search for all text files:

find /home -name "*.txt"

Search for directories only:

find . -type d

Search for regular files:

find . -type f

docs.title: Searching by Size
docs.text:
Find files larger than 100 MB:

find / -size +100M

Find files smaller than 10 KB:

find /home -size -10k

docs.title: Searching by Modification Time
docs.text:
Find files modified within the last day:

find . -mtime -1

Find files older than 30 days:

find . -mtime +30

docs.title: Using locate
docs.text:
The locate command searches a pre-built database instead of scanning the filesystem.

Example:

locate ssh_config

Because it uses a database, it is usually much faster than find.

If recently created files do not appear, update the database:

sudo updatedb

Note: locate may not be installed by default on all Linux distributions.

docs.title: Finding Commands
docs.text: Linux provides several commands for locating executables and identifying command types.

docs.title: which
docs.text:
Displays the location of an executable in your PATH.

Example:

which ls

Output:

/usr/bin/ls

docs.title: whereis
docs.text:
Displays the executable, source files and manual pages (where available).

Example:

whereis ssh

Example output:

ssh: /usr/bin/ssh /usr/share/man/man1/ssh.1.gz

docs.title: type
docs.text:
Shows how the shell interprets a command.

Example:

type cd

Output:

cd is a shell builtin

Example:

type ls

Output:

ls is /usr/bin/ls

docs.title: Hidden Files
docs.text:
Hidden files begin with a period (.).

Examples:

.bashrc
.profile
.gitconfig

To display hidden files:

ls -a

To include detailed information:

ls -la

Hidden files are commonly used to store configuration settings.

docs.title: Understanding Links
docs.text:
Linux supports two types of links:

  • Hard links
  • Symbolic (soft) links

Both provide additional ways to reference files.

docs.title: Hard Links
docs.text:
A hard link creates another directory entry for the same file.

Create a hard link:

ln notes.txt notes-hardlink.txt

Display the files:

ls -li

Example:

123456 notes.txt
123456 notes-hardlink.txt

Notice both files share the same inode number.

Changes made to either file affect the same underlying data.

docs.title: Hard Link Characteristics
docs.text:
• Shares the same inode
  • Appears as another copy of the file
  • Continues to work if the original filename is deleted
  • Cannot normally link directories
  • Cannot span different filesystems

docs.title: Symbolic Links
docs.text:
A symbolic link (or soft link) is a shortcut that points to another file or directory.

Create a symbolic link:

ln -s notes.txt notes-link.txt

Display the result:

ls -l

Example:

notes-link.txt -> notes.txt

docs.title: Symbolic Link Characteristics
docs.text:
• Points to another file
  • Has its own inode
  • Can span filesystems
  • Can point to directories
  • Becomes broken if the original file is removed

docs.title: Hard Links vs Symbolic Links
docs.text: Feature Hard Link Symbolic Link Shares inode ✅ Yes ❌ No Can cross filesystems ❌ No ✅ Yes Can link directories ❌ Normally no ✅ Yes Works if original filename is removed ✅ Yes ❌ No

docs.title: Removing Links
docs.text:
Remove a symbolic link:

rm notes-link.txt

This removes only the link, not the original file.

The same command removes hard links.

The original file remains until all hard links have been removed.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:

✔ Use locate when speed is important.

✔ Use symbolic links for shortcuts.

✔ Verify links using:

ls -l

docs.title: Lesson 01 - Understanding Linux Users and Groups
docs.text:
Estimated time: 45–60 minutes

Prerequisites: - Module 00 – Introduction to Linux - Module 01 – Command Line Fundamentals - Module 02 – Linux Filesystem Administration

Difficulty: Beginner

Hands-on exercises: Yes

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Linux is a multi-user operating system, designed from the ground up to allow many users to work on the same system safely and securely.

Every file, process and service belongs to a user and, usually, to a group. Understanding how users and groups work is fundamental to administering Linux systems, whether you're managing a single Raspberry Pi or hundreds of cloud servers.

In this lesson you'll learn how Linux identifies users, how groups simplify permission management, and how to inspect account information from the command line.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • Explain why Linux uses users and groups.
  • Distinguish between users and groups.
  • Understand User IDs (UIDs) and Group IDs (GIDs).
  • Identify system accounts and regular user accounts.
  • View information about the current user.
  • Examine user and group information stored by Linux.

docs.title: Why Linux Uses Users
docs.text:
Linux assumes that multiple people may use the same computer at different times—or even simultaneously.

Each user has their own:

  • Home directory
  • Files
  • Settings
  • Password
  • Permissions

This separation helps keep data secure and prevents users from interfering with each other's work.

For example:

/home
├── alice
├── bob
└── james

Each user has their own workspace inside the /home directory.

docs.title: What is a User?
docs.text:
A user represents an individual account on the system.

Every user has:

  • A username
  • A password (or another authentication method)
  • A unique User ID (UID)
  • A primary group
  • A home directory
  • A default login shell

For example:

Username: james
UID:      1000
Home:     /home/james
Shell:    /bin/bash

Linux uses the UID internally rather than the username to identify users.

docs.title: What is a Group?
docs.text:
A group is a collection of users.

Groups simplify permission management by allowing multiple users to share access to files and directories.

For example:

developers
├── alice
├── bob
└── james

Instead of granting permissions to each user individually, permissions can be assigned to the group.

docs.title: Primary and Secondary Groups
docs.text:
Every Linux user belongs to at least one group.

There are two types of group membership:

docs.title: Primary Group
docs.text:
Every user has one primary group.

Example:

User: james
Primary group: james

Files created by the user normally belong to this group.

docs.title: Secondary Groups
docs.text:
A user may also belong to additional groups.

Example:

User: james

Groups:
- james
- docker
- sudo

Secondary groups provide additional permissions without changing the primary group.

docs.title: User IDs (UID)
docs.text:
Every user has a unique numerical identifier called a User ID (UID).

Typical ranges are:

UID Range Purpose 0 Root user 1–999 System and service accounts (distribution dependent) 1000+ Regular user accounts

The root user always has a UID of 0.

docs.title: Group IDs (GID)
docs.text:
Groups also have unique numerical identifiers called Group IDs (GIDs).

Linux uses GIDs internally in the same way it uses UIDs for users.

docs.title: The Root User
docs.text:
The root account is the Linux administrator.

Root can:

  • Access every file
  • Modify system configuration
  • Install software
  • Create and remove users
  • Change permissions
  • Start and stop services

Because root has unrestricted access, administrators normally use sudo rather than logging in directly as root.

docs.title: System Accounts
docs.text:
Not every account belongs to a person.

Linux creates many accounts for running services.

Examples include:

www-data
daemon
nobody
systemd-network

These accounts improve security by allowing services to run with only the permissions they require.

docs.title: Viewing Your Current User
docs.text:
Use the whoami command to display the current user.

whoami

Example:

james

docs.title: Displaying User Information
docs.text:
The id command displays detailed information about the current user.

id

Example:

uid=1000(james)
gid=1000(james)
groups=1000(james),27(sudo),998(docker)

This shows:

  • User ID
  • Primary Group ID
  • Group memberships

docs.title: Displaying Logged-in Users
docs.text:
To see who is currently logged in:

who

Example:

james    pts/0    09:45
admin    pts/1    10:12

docs.title: Viewing Group Membership
docs.text:
To display the groups for the current user:

groups

Example:

james sudo docker

docs.title: Where User Information is Stored
docs.text:
Linux stores account information in text files.

Common files include:

File Purpose /etc/passwd User account information /etc/group Group information /etc/shadow Encrypted password information

You will explore these files in the next lesson.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
✔ Use standard user accounts for everyday work.

✔ Use sudo only when administrative privileges are required.

✔ Assign permissions using groups rather than individual users whenever possible.

✔ Avoid logging in directly as the root user.

✔ Regularly review user accounts and group memberships.

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this lesson you learned:

  • Why Linux uses users and groups.
  • The difference between users and groups.
  • What UIDs and GIDs are.
  • The role of the root account.
  • The purpose of system accounts.
  • How to identify the current user and group memberships.

In the next lesson, you'll learn how to create, modify and manage user accounts and groups using common Linux administration commands.

docs.title: Lesson 02 - Managing Users and Groups
docs.text:
Estimated time: 75–90 minutes

Prerequisites: - Lesson 01 – Understanding Linux Users and Groups

Difficulty: Beginner

Hands-on exercises: Yes

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Linux administrators regularly create, modify and remove user accounts as people join, leave or change roles within an organisation.

This lesson introduces the tools used to manage users and groups safely from the command line. You'll also learn where Linux stores account information and how to inspect it.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • Create user accounts
  • Modify existing users
  • Delete user accounts
  • Create and manage groups
  • Add users to groups
  • Understand Linux account databases
  • Verify user and group configuration

docs.title: Linux Account Files
docs.text:
Linux stores account information in several important files.

File Purpose /etc/passwd User account information /etc/shadow Encrypted passwords /etc/group Group information /etc/gshadow Secure group information

View the contents of /etc/passwd:

cat /etc/passwd

Example:

root:x:0:0:root:/root:/bin/bash
james:x:1000:1000:James Roberts:/home/james:/bin/bash

Each line contains information about one user account.

docs.title: Creating a User
docs.text:
Create a new user with:

sudo useradd alice

Verify the account exists:

id alice

Example:

uid=1001(alice) gid=1001(alice)

docs.title: Creating a Home Directory
docs.text:
Some distributions automatically create a home directory, while others require the -m option.

sudo useradd -m alice

The user's home directory will be:

/home/alice

docs.title: Setting a Password
docs.text:
Assign a password using:

sudo passwd alice

Example:

New password:
Retype new password:
passwd: password updated successfully

docs.title: Viewing User Information
docs.text:
Display information about a user:

id alice

Display group membership:

groups alice

docs.title: Modifying a User
docs.text:
Use usermod to change account settings.

Example:

sudo usermod -s /bin/bash alice

This changes the user's default shell.

Change the home directory:

sudo usermod -d /home/newhome alice

docs.title: Locking and Unlocking Accounts
docs.text:
Lock an account:

sudo passwd -l alice

Unlock it again:

sudo passwd -u alice

This is useful when temporarily disabling an account without deleting it.

docs.title: Deleting a User
docs.text:
Delete an account:

sudo userdel alice

Remove the account and its home directory:

sudo userdel -r alice

Use the -r option carefully, as it permanently removes the user's files.

docs.title: Creating Groups
docs.text:
Create a group:

sudo groupadd developers

Verify:

getent group developers

Example:

developers:x:1001:

docs.title: Adding a User to a Group
docs.text:
Add an existing user to a secondary group:

sudo usermod -aG developers alice

The options mean:

  • -a = append
  • -G = supplementary groups

Verify:

groups alice

Example:

alice : alice developers

docs.title: Removing a User from a Group
docs.text:
Remove a user from a supplementary group:

sudo gpasswd -d alice developers

docs.title: Deleting a Group
docs.text:
Delete a group:

sudo groupdel developers

docs.title: Viewing Login Information
docs.text:
Display the currently logged-in users:

who

Display your username:

whoami

Display your identity:

id

docs.title: Useful Administration Commands
docs.text: Command Purpose useradd Create users usermod Modify users userdel Delete users passwd Manage passwords groupadd Create groups groupdel Delete groups groups Display group membership id Display user identity whoami Display current username who Display logged-in users

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
✔ Create a home directory for each user.

✔ Assign strong passwords.

✔ Use groups to manage permissions rather than assigning users individually.

✔ Lock accounts instead of deleting them if access may be required again.

✔ Remove unused accounts promptly.

✔ Review user and group membership regularly.

docs.text:

  2. Which file stores user account information?
  3. What command sets a user's password?
  4. How do you add a user to a secondary group?
  5. Which command displays a user's UID and GID?
  6. What does the -r option do when used with userdel?

docs.title: Summary
docs.text:
In this lesson you learned how to:

  • Create user accounts
  • Set passwords
  • Modify users
  • Delete users
  • Create groups
  • Add users to groups
  • Understand the Linux account database
  • Verify account configuration

In the next lesson, you'll learn how Linux uses passwords, account policies and sudo to provide secure administrative access.

docs.title: Lesson 03 - Passwords and Administrative Access
docs.text:
Estimated time: 60–90 minutes

Prerequisites: - Lesson 01 – Understanding Linux Users and Groups - Lesson 02 – Managing Users and Groups

Difficulty: Beginner to Intermediate

Hands-on exercises: Yes

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Linux systems use authentication and authorisation controls to protect system resources.

Authentication answers the question:

"Who are you?"

Authorisation answers the question:

"What are you allowed to do?"

In this lesson you will learn how Linux manages passwords, how password policies are controlled, and how administrators safely perform privileged tasks using sudo.

docs.title: Learning Objectives
docs.text:
By the end of this lesson you will be able to:

  • Understand how Linux stores passwords securely.
  • Change and manage user passwords.
  • Understand password ageing policies.
  • Lock and unlock accounts.
  • Use sudo for administrative tasks.
  • Understand the difference between normal and privileged access.
  • Configure administrative permissions safely.

docs.title: Linux Authentication
docs.text:
When a user logs into Linux, the system verifies their identity.

The process involves:

User
 |
 | Username + Password
 |
 v
Authentication System
 |
 v
Linux System
 |
 v
User Session

Linux checks:

  • Username
  • Password
  • Account status
  • Login restrictions
  • Access policies

docs.title: Password Storage
docs.text:
Linux does not store passwords as plain text.

Password information is stored in:

/etc/shadow

View the file:

sudo cat /etc/shadow

Example:

james:$6$randomhashvalue:20100:0:99999:7:::

The password field contains a cryptographic hash.

A hash is:

  • One-way
  • Not reversible
  • Designed to protect passwords

docs.title: The /etc/passwd File
docs.text:
User account information is stored in:

/etc/passwd

Example:

james:x:1000:1000:James:/home/james:/bin/bash

The x indicates that the password is stored separately in /etc/shadow.

docs.title: Changing Passwords
docs.text:
Users can change their own password:

passwd

Administrators can change another user's password:

sudo passwd username

Example:

sudo passwd alice

docs.title: Password Expiration
docs.text:
Linux can enforce password ageing policies.

View password information:

sudo chage -l username

Example:

Last password change                    : Jul 01, 2026
Password expires                        : Sep 29, 2026
Password inactive                       : never

docs.title: Changing Password Policies
docs.text:
Force a user to change their password on next login:

sudo chage -d 0 username

Set password expiry:

sudo chage -M 90 username

This requires the user to change their password every 90 days.

docs.title: Locking User Accounts
docs.text:
A user account can be temporarily disabled.

Lock:

sudo passwd -l username

Example:

sudo passwd -l alice

Unlock:

sudo passwd -u username

Locking is useful when:

  • A user leaves temporarily
  • Investigating security issues
  • Disabling unused accounts

docs.title: What is sudo?
docs.text:
sudo means:

Super User DO

It allows authorised users to run commands with elevated privileges.

Example:

Normal user:

apt update

May fail:

Permission denied

Using sudo:

sudo apt update

Runs the command as root.

docs.title: Why Use sudo?
docs.text:
The recommended approach is:

Normal User
     |
     |
   sudo
     |
     |
Administrator Task

Rather than:

Login directly as root

Benefits:

  • Better security
  • Audit trail
  • Reduced mistakes
  • Least privilege access

docs.title: Checking sudo Access
docs.text:
Check if your user can use sudo:

groups

Example:

james sudo docker

Users in the sudo group can normally perform administrative tasks.

docs.title: Running Commands with sudo
docs.text:
Example:

View protected files:

sudo cat /etc/shadow

Install software:

sudo apt install nginx

Restart services:

sudo systemctl restart ssh

docs.title: Switching Users
docs.text:
The su command allows you to switch users.

Example:

su alice

Switch to root:

su -

However, using sudo is generally preferred.

docs.title: sudo Configuration
docs.text:
The sudo configuration file is:

/etc/sudoers

Never edit this file directly.

Use:

sudo visudo

visudo checks the configuration before saving.

This prevents syntax errors that could remove administrator access.

docs.title: Example sudo Configuration
docs.text:
Example:

alice ALL=(ALL) ALL

Meaning:

  • User: alice
  • Host: ALL
  • Can run commands as: ALL users
  • Commands: ALL

docs.title: Least Privilege Principle
docs.text:
Users should only receive the permissions they need.

Example:

A web administrator may need:

restart web service

They do not necessarily need:

full root access

Good security practice:

✔ Give required access only

✔ Review permissions regularly

✔ Remove unused accounts

✔ Avoid shared administrator accounts

docs.text:
Run:

whoami

Record:

Username:

Run:

id

Record:

UID:

docs.title: Task 2 - Create a Test User
docs.text:
Create:

sudo useradd -m testuser

Set password:

sudo passwd testuser

Verify:

id testuser

docs.title: Task 3 - Test Account Locking
docs.text:
Lock the account:

sudo passwd -l testuser

Check:

sudo passwd -S testuser

Unlock:

sudo passwd -u testuser

docs.title: Task 4 - Review Password Policy
docs.text:
Run:

sudo chage -l testuser

Review the settings.

  4. What does sudo allow a user to do?

  6. What is the purpose of least privilege?

docs.text:
This practical lab combines the skills learned throughout the Users and Groups module.

You will perform common Linux administration tasks including:

The scenario is based on a common real-world administration task: preparing a Linux server for a new team.

docs.title: Scenario
docs.text:
You are a Linux administrator managing a development server.

A new development team requires access.

The requirements are:

  • Create a development group
  • Create user accounts
  • Assign users to the correct groups
  • Configure passwords
  • Verify access
  • Remove access when required

docs.title: Lab Environment
docs.text:
Before starting, check your current account:

whoami

Check your permissions:

id

Confirm you can use sudo:

sudo -v

docs.title: Task 1 - Create the Development Group
docs.text:
Create a group called:

developers

Command:

sudo groupadd developers

Verify:

getent group developers

Expected output:

developers:x:1001:

docs.title: Task 2 - Create User Accounts
docs.text:
Create two users:

alice
bob

Create their home directories:

sudo useradd -m alice
sudo useradd -m bob

Verify:

id alice
id bob

docs.title: Task 3 - Set User Passwords
docs.text:
Set passwords:

sudo passwd alice
sudo passwd bob

Confirm the accounts exist:

cat /etc/passwd | grep -E "alice|bob"

docs.title: Task 4 - Add Users to the Development Group
docs.text:
Add both users to the developers group:

sudo usermod -aG developers alice
sudo usermod -aG developers bob

Verify:

groups alice
groups bob

Expected:

alice : alice developers

bob : bob developers

docs.title: Task 5 - Create a Shared Development Directory
docs.text:
Create:

sudo mkdir /development

Assign ownership to the developers group:

sudo chown root:developers /development

Set permissions:

sudo chmod 770 /development

Check:

ls -ld /development

Expected:

drwxrwx--- root developers /development

docs.title: Task 6 - Test User Access
docs.text:
Switch to the alice account:

su - alice

Check identity:

whoami

Try creating a file:

touch /development/alice-test.txt

List the directory:

ls -l /development

Exit:

exit

docs.title: Task 7 - Review Account Information
docs.text:
Check users:

id alice
id bob

Review groups:

getent group developers

Review password status:

sudo passwd -S alice

docs.title: Task 8 - Configure Administrative Access
docs.text:
Add alice to the sudo group:

sudo usermod -aG sudo alice

Verify:

groups alice

The output should include:

sudo

docs.title: Task 9 - Test sudo Access
docs.text:
Switch to alice:

su - alice

Run:

sudo whoami

Expected:

root

Exit:

exit

docs.title: Task 10 - Disable an Account
docs.text:
Temporarily disable bob:

sudo passwd -l bob

Check status:

sudo passwd -S bob

Unlock:

sudo passwd -u bob

docs.title: Task 11 - Remove Test Accounts
docs.text:
Remove users:

sudo userdel -r alice
sudo userdel -r bob

Remove group:

sudo groupdel developers

Verify:

getent group developers

No output should be returned.

Possible causes:

  • User not in the correct group
  • Incorrect permissions
  • Incorrect ownership

docs.title: Problem 2

Check:

groups username

Possible causes:

  • User not in sudo group
  • Incorrect sudo configuration

docs.title: Lesson 01 - Understanding Linux Processes

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A Linux system is made up of many running processes.

Every command you execute, every application you start, and every system service running in the background is a process.

Understanding processes is a fundamental Linux administration skill because it allows administrators to:

  • Monitor system activity
  • Identify resource usage
  • Troubleshoot problems
  • Stop unwanted applications
  • Investigate service failures

docs.title: What is a Process?
docs.text:
A process is a running instance of a program.

When a program is stored on disk, it is simply a file.

When that program is started, Linux loads it into memory and creates a process.

Example:

Program:

/usr/bin/nginx

Running process:

nginx process

docs.title: A program is:
docs.text:
• A file stored on disk
  • Contains instructions for the computer

docs.title: A process is:
docs.text:
• A running copy of a program
  • Uses CPU and memory resources
  • Has a unique identifier

Example:

Program:

/usr/bin/nginx

Running process:

nginx PID 1234

docs.title: Process IDs (PID)
docs.text:
Every running process in Linux receives a unique number called a:

Process ID (PID)

The PID allows administrators to identify and manage individual processes.

Example:

PID Command 1 systemd 550 sshd 1200 nginx 2500 bash

No two running processes have the same PID.

docs.title: The Init Process
docs.text:
The first process started by the Linux kernel is:

PID 1

On modern Linux systems this is normally:

systemd

Check PID 1:

ps -p 1

Example output:

PID TTY      TIME CMD
1   ?        00:00:02 systemd

The PID 1 process is responsible for:

  • Starting system services
  • Managing background services
  • Handling system startup
  • Replacing failed processes

docs.title: Parent and Child Processes
docs.text:
Processes can create other processes.

The process that creates another process is called the:

Parent Process

The new process is called the:

Child Process

Example:

systemd
 |
 ├── sshd
 |    |
 |    └── bash
 |
 └── cron

In this example:

  • systemd is the parent of sshd
  • sshd is the parent of bash

docs.title: Viewing Processes
docs.text:
The ps command displays running processes.

Basic usage:

ps

Example:

PID TTY          TIME CMD
2301 pts/0    00:00:00 bash
2450 pts/0    00:00:00 ps

By default, ps only shows processes from your current terminal.

docs.title: Viewing All Processes
docs.text:
To view all running processes:

ps aux

Example:

USER       PID %CPU %MEM COMMAND

root         1  0.0  0.5 /sbin/init
root       500  0.1  1.2 sshd
james     2200  0.0  0.3 bash

Information shown:

Column Meaning USER Owner of process PID Process ID %CPU CPU usage %MEM Memory usage COMMAND Program running

docs.title: Viewing Process Relationships
docs.text:
The pstree command displays processes in a tree format.

Example:

pstree

Output:

systemd
├─sshd
│ └─bash
├─cron
└─nginx

This makes parent and child relationships easier to understand.

docs.title: Searching for Processes
docs.text:
The pgrep command searches for processes by name.

Example:

pgrep ssh

Output:

500

This returns the PID of matching processes.

docs.title: Monitoring Processes
docs.text:
The top command provides a live view of system activity.

Run:

top

Example:

PID USER      %CPU %MEM COMMAND

1200 root      5.0  2.1 nginx
2200 james     1.0  0.5 bash

Useful information:

  • CPU usage
  • Memory usage
  • Running processes
  • System load

Exit top:

q

docs.title: Background Processes
docs.text:
Linux can run commands in the background.

Example:

sleep 300 &

The & symbol runs the command in the background.

Example output:

[1] 3456

Where:

3456 = Process ID

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Linux systems run many processes at the same time.

Administrators need to understand how to:

  • View running processes
  • Identify resource usage
  • Find specific processes
  • Run commands in the background
  • Control and stop processes safely

Process management is an important skill for troubleshooting performance issues and maintaining system stability.

docs.title: Viewing Processes
docs.text: Linux provides several commands for viewing running processes.

docs.title: ps Command
docs.text:
The ps command displays information about running processes.

Basic usage:

ps

Example output:

PID TTY          TIME CMD
1234 pts/0    00:00:00 bash
5678 pts/0    00:00:01 ps

Information shown:

Column Meaning PID Process ID TTY Terminal TIME CPU time used CMD Command

docs.title: Viewing All Processes
docs.text:
To view all running processes:

ps aux

Example:

USER       PID %CPU %MEM COMMAND
root         1  0.0  1.2 systemd
james     1234  0.1  0.5 bash

Important columns:

Column Meaning USER Process owner PID Process ID %CPU CPU usage %MEM Memory usage COMMAND Running command

docs.title: Using pgrep
docs.text:
The pgrep command searches for processes by name.

Example:

pgrep ssh

Output:

742

This returns the process ID.

docs.title: Using ps with grep
docs.text:
Example:

ps aux | grep ssh

This searches the process list.

Example output:

root 742 0.0 sshd

docs.title: Process Information
docs.text:
To view details about a process:

ps -fp PID

Example:

ps -fp 742

Output:

UID   PID  PPID CMD
root  742    1  sshd

Information:

Field Meaning PID Process ID PPID Parent Process ID CMD Command

docs.title: Parent and Child Processes
docs.text:
Processes can create other processes.

Example:

systemd
 |
 ├── sshd
 |    |
 |    └── bash
 |
 └── cron

View process relationships:

pstree

This shows the hierarchy of processes.

docs.title: Background Processes
docs.text:
Commands normally run in the foreground.

Example:

sleep 60

The terminal waits until the command finishes.

To run a command in the background:

sleep 300 &

Example output:

[1] 12345

The number returned is the process ID.

docs.title: Viewing Background Jobs
docs.text:
Show running background jobs:

jobs

Example:

[1]+ Running sleep 300 &

docs.title: Bringing Jobs to the Foreground
docs.text:
Move a background job back:

fg

Example:

fg %1

docs.title: Sending Processes to the Background
docs.text:
A running command can be moved into the background.

Press:

CTRL + Z

Then:

bg

Example:

sleep 300

CTRL + Z

bg

docs.title: Process Signals
docs.text:
Linux controls processes using signals.

Common signals:

Signal Number Purpose SIGHUP 1 Reload configuration SIGTERM 15 Graceful shutdown SIGKILL 9 Force termination

docs.title: Using kill
docs.text:
Terminate a process:

kill PID

Example:

kill 12345

This sends:

SIGTERM

docs.title: Force Stopping Processes
docs.text:
If a process does not stop:

kill -9 PID

Example:

kill -9 12345

SIGKILL immediately stops the process.

Use carefully because the application cannot clean up.

docs.title: Using pkill
docs.text:
Kill processes by name:

pkill process_name

Example:

pkill sleep

docs.title: top
docs.text:
The top command provides real-time process monitoring.

Run:

top

Shows:

  • CPU usage
  • Memory usage
  • Running processes
  • System load

docs.title: htop
docs.text:
If installed:

htop

Provides an interactive interface.

Install:

sudo apt install htop

docs.title: Process Priority
docs.text:
Linux allows processes to have different priorities.

Priority is controlled using:

nice
renice

View priority:

ps -el

docs.title: Starting a Process with Priority
docs.text:
Example:

nice -n 10 command

Higher nice values mean lower priority.

docs.title: Changing Process Priority
docs.text:
Example:

renice 10 -p PID

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Modern Linux systems use systemd to manage system startup, background services and system processes.

Services such as web servers, databases, SSH access and monitoring tools are controlled by systemd.

Understanding systemd is an essential Linux administration skill because it allows administrators to:

  • Start and stop services
  • Enable services at boot
  • Check service status
  • Investigate failures
  • Review service logs

docs.title: What is systemd?
docs.text:
systemd is the service manager used by most modern Linux distributions.

Examples:

  • Ubuntu
  • Debian
  • Rocky Linux
  • Fedora
  • Red Hat Enterprise Linux

systemd is responsible for:

  • Starting services during boot
  • Managing running services
  • Monitoring service health
  • Handling dependencies
  • Recording service events

The systemd process normally runs as:

PID 1

Check:

ps -p 1

Example:

PID TTY      TIME CMD
1   ?        00:00:03 systemd

docs.title: Services
docs.text:
A service is a background process that provides functionality to the system.

Examples:

Service Purpose ssh Remote administration nginx Web server cron Scheduled tasks docker Container management networking Network management

Services normally run without user interaction.

docs.title: Service Units
docs.text:
systemd manages services using unit files.

Common unit types:

Unit Type Purpose .service System services .timer Scheduled tasks .socket Network sockets .mount Filesystem mounts

Example:

ssh.service

docs.title: Checking Service Status
docs.text:
The main command for managing services is:

systemctl

To check a service:

systemctl status ssh

Example:

● ssh.service - OpenBSD Secure Shell server
     Loaded: loaded
     Active: active (running)

Important information:

  • Service name
  • Current state
  • Process ID
  • Recent log messages

docs.title: Service States
docs.text:
Common service states:

State Meaning active (running) Service is running inactive Service is stopped failed Service failed activating Service starting deactivating Service stopping

docs.title: Starting Services
docs.text:
Start a service:

sudo systemctl start service_name

Example:

sudo systemctl start nginx

The service starts immediately.

docs.title: Stopping Services
docs.text:
Stop a service:

sudo systemctl stop service_name

Example:

sudo systemctl stop nginx

The service stops immediately.

docs.title: Restarting Services
docs.text:
Restart a service:

sudo systemctl restart service_name

Example:

sudo systemctl restart ssh

Restarting is commonly used after configuration changes.

docs.title: Reloading Services
docs.text:
Some services support configuration reloads without stopping.

Example:

sudo systemctl reload nginx

This applies configuration changes while keeping the service running.

docs.title: Enabling Services at Boot
docs.text:
A service can be configured to start automatically when Linux boots.

Enable:

sudo systemctl enable service_name

Example:

sudo systemctl enable docker

docs.title: Disabling Services at Boot
docs.text:
Prevent automatic startup:

sudo systemctl disable service_name

Example:

sudo systemctl disable nginx

docs.title: Checking Enabled Services
docs.text:
View enabled services:

systemctl list-unit-files --type=service

Example:

ssh.service       enabled
docker.service    enabled
nginx.service     disabled

docs.title: Listing Running Services
docs.text:
View active services:

systemctl list-units --type=service

Example:

ssh.service
cron.service
docker.service

docs.title: Finding Service Files
docs.text:
Service files are stored in:

/usr/lib/systemd/system/

and:

/etc/systemd/system/

Example:

ls /etc/systemd/system

docs.title: Viewing Service Dependencies
docs.text:
Services can depend on other services.

View dependencies:

systemctl list-dependencies service_name

Example:

systemctl list-dependencies ssh
