docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Linux systems generate a large amount of information about what is happening on the system.

This information is stored in logs.

Logs help administrators:

  • Troubleshoot problems
  • Investigate service failures
  • Monitor system activity
  • Identify security events
  • Understand system behaviour

Modern Linux systems use systemd-journald to collect and manage system logs.

The main tool used to view these logs is:

journalctl
Linux Logging

Linux records information about:

System startup
Running services
User activity
Hardware events
Application messages
Security events

Examples of logs:

Log Type    Example
Authentication  SSH login attempts
System  Kernel messages
Services    Service startup failures
Applications    Application errors
Traditional Log Files

Historically, Linux stored logs in:

/var/log

View the directory:

ls /var/log

Common log files:

File    Purpose
auth.log    Authentication events
syslog  General system messages
kern.log    Kernel messages
dpkg.log    Package management events

Example:

cat /var/log/syslog
systemd Journal

Modern Linux distributions use the systemd journal.

The journal collects messages from:

The kernel
System services
Applications
User sessions

The journal is managed by:

systemd-journald

Check the service:

systemctl status systemd-journald
Viewing Logs with journalctl

The basic command:

journalctl

displays the system journal.

Example:

Jul 31 10:15:01 server systemd[1]: Started SSH service.
Jul 31 10:15:02 server sshd[500]: Accepted password login.
Viewing Recent Logs

Show the latest log entries:

journalctl -n

Example:

journalctl -n 50

This displays the last 50 entries.

Following Live Logs

Similar to tail -f:

journalctl -f

This displays new log entries as they appear.

Useful when:

Starting services
Testing changes
Troubleshooting problems

Exit using:

CTRL + C
Viewing Logs for a Service

To view logs for a specific service:

journalctl -u service_name

Example:

journalctl -u ssh

This shows only SSH service logs.

Viewing Recent Service Failures

Show recent errors:

journalctl -p err

Example output:

Failed to start nginx.service

Priority levels include:

Level   Meaning
emerg   System unusable

This lesson covers updating Linux systems using common package management tools.

docs.title: Why Update Linux Systems?
docs.text:
Regular updates help maintain:

  • System security
  • Application reliability
  • Hardware compatibility
  • Performance
  • Vendor support

Unpatched systems may contain:

  • Security vulnerabilities
  • Software bugs
  • Outdated components
  • Unsupported versions

docs.title: Package Updates vs Distribution Upgrades
docs.text: There are different types of updates.

docs.title: Package Update
docs.text:
Updates installed software packages.

Example:

nginx version 1.24
        |
        v
nginx version 1.26

Usually includes:

  • Bug fixes
  • Security patches
  • Minor improvements

docs.title: Distribution Upgrade
docs.text:
Moves the operating system to a newer release.

Example:

Ubuntu 24.04 LTS

        |

Ubuntu 26.04 LTS

Distribution upgrades require more planning because they can affect:

  • Applications
  • Configuration files
  • Services
  • Hardware compatibility

docs.title: Updating Debian and Ubuntu Systems
docs.text:
Debian-based systems use:

apt

The update process normally has two stages:

  1. Refresh package information
  2. Install available updates

docs.title: Updating Package Information
docs.text:
Run:

sudo apt update

This downloads the latest package information from repositories.

Example:

Hit:1 http://archive.ubuntu.com
Get:2 security updates
Reading package lists...

This does not install updates.

It only checks what updates are available.

docs.title: Installing Updates
docs.text:
Install available updates:

sudo apt upgrade

The system will:

  • Download updated packages
  • Install new versions
  • Keep existing configuration

Example:

20 packages can be upgraded.

docs.title: Full Upgrade
docs.text:
For more complex updates:

sudo apt full-upgrade

This allows:

  • Installing new dependencies
  • Removing conflicting packages
  • Updating core components

Use carefully on production systems.

docs.title: Checking Available Updates
docs.text:
View available upgrades:

apt list --upgradable

Example:

nginx
openssl
curl

docs.title: Removing Unused Packages After Updates
docs.text:
Old dependencies may no longer be required.

Remove unused packages:

sudo apt autoremove

Clean downloaded package files:

sudo apt clean

docs.title: Updating Red Hat and Rocky Linux Systems
docs.text:
Red Hat-based systems use:

dnf

docs.title: Checking Available Updates
docs.text:
Run:

dnf check-update

This checks repositories for available updates.

docs.title: Installing Updates
docs.text:
Update the system:

sudo dnf upgrade

or:

sudo dnf update

Both commands update installed packages.

docs.title: Viewing Update History
docs.text: Package managers keep records of changes.

docs.title: Debian / Ubuntu
docs.text:
View package logs:

cat /var/log/apt/history.log

docs.title: Red Hat / Rocky Linux
docs.text:
View DNF history:

dnf history

Example:

ID   Command
1    Install nginx
2    Upgrade packages

docs.title: Security Updates
docs.text:
Security updates are especially important.

They fix vulnerabilities in:

  • Operating system components
  • Libraries
  • Applications
  • Services

docs.title: Checking Security Updates on Ubuntu
docs.text:
Install update tools:

sudo apt install unattended-upgrades

Enable automatic security updates:

sudo dpkg-reconfigure unattended-upgrades

docs.title: Update Planning
docs.text: Before updating production systems:

docs.title: Check Current State
docs.text:
Review:

  • Running services
  • Disk space
  • System health
  • Current versions

Commands:

systemctl --failed

df -h

docs.title: Backup Important Data
docs.text:
Before major updates:

  • Backup configuration files
  • Backup application data
  • Confirm recovery procedures

docs.title: Test Updates
docs.text:
Where possible:

  1. Test updates in development
  2. Review changes
  3. Schedule maintenance window
  4. Apply updates

docs.title: Reboot Requirements
docs.text:
Some updates require a reboot.

Common examples:

  • Kernel updates
  • Hardware drivers
  • Core system libraries

Check if reboot is required:

  • Incorrect configuration

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Linux package managers rely on software repositories to locate and download software packages.

Repositories provide a controlled source of software that has been tested and packaged for a specific Linux distribution.

Understanding repositories is important for Linux administrators because they control:

  • Where software is downloaded from
  • Which software versions are available
  • How systems receive updates
  • Which software sources are trusted

docs.title: What is a Software Repository?
docs.text:
A software repository is a server location that stores software packages and related information.

A repository contains:

  • Software packages
  • Package versions
  • Dependency information
  • Security updates
  • Package metadata

Example:

Linux System

      |
      |
 Package Manager

      |
      |
 Software Repository

      |
      |
 Package Download

docs.title: Why Use Repositories?
docs.text: Repositories provide several benefits:

docs.title: Security
docs.text:
Packages are usually:

  • Signed by trusted providers
  • Verified before installation
  • Maintained with security updates

docs.title: Dependency Management
docs.text:
Repositories provide required supporting software.

Example:

Application

requires:

Library A
Library B
Configuration Package

The package manager automatically downloads dependencies.

docs.title: Software Updates
docs.text:
Repositories allow administrators to:

  • Receive security fixes
  • Update applications
  • Maintain supported versions

docs.title: Repository Components
docs.text: A repository normally contains:

docs.title: Packages
docs.text:

Example:

nginx.deb

docs.title: Metadata
docs.text:
Information about packages:

  • Name
  • Version
  • Description
  • Dependencies
  • Available updates

docs.title: Digital Signatures
docs.text:
Used to verify:

  • Package authenticity
  • Repository trust
  • Package integrity

docs.title: Debian and Ubuntu Repositories
docs.text:
Debian-based systems use:

apt

Repository configuration is stored in:

/etc/apt/sources.list

Additional repositories:

/etc/apt/sources.list.d/

docs.title: Viewing APT Repository Configuration
docs.text:
View configured repositories:

cat /etc/apt/sources.list

Example:

deb http://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu noble main

docs.title: Updating Repository Information
docs.text:
After changing repository settings:

Run:

sudo apt update

This downloads the latest repository information.

docs.title: APT Repository Format
docs.text:
A repository entry contains several parts:

Example:

deb http://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu noble main

Breakdown:

Section Meaning deb Package type URL Repository location noble Distribution release main Repository component

docs.title: Repository Components in Ubuntu
docs.text:
Ubuntu repositories are divided into sections.

Common components:

Component Purpose main Officially supported software universe Community maintained software restricted Proprietary drivers multiverse Software with licensing restrictions

docs.title: Adding Software Repositories
docs.text:
Sometimes software is not available in the default repositories.

Administrators may add additional repositories.

Examples:

  • Vendor repositories
  • Internal company repositories
  • Third-party software sources

Before adding repositories, consider:

  • Is the source trusted?
  • Is it maintained?
  • Does it provide security updates?
  • Is it required?

docs.title: Personal Package Archives (PPA)
docs.text:
Ubuntu supports additional repositories called:

PPA - Personal Package Archive

Example:

sudo add-apt-repository ppa:name/repository

Update package information:

sudo apt update

docs.title: Removing Repositories
docs.text:
Repositories can be removed when no longer required.

Example:

sudo add-apt-repository --remove ppa:name/repository

Then update:

sudo apt update

docs.title: Red Hat and Rocky Linux Repositories
docs.text:
Red Hat-based systems use:

dnf

Repository configuration is stored in:

/etc/yum.repos.d/

docs.title: Viewing DNF Repositories
docs.text:
List enabled repositories:

dnf repolist

Example:

repo id
baseos
appstream

docs.title: Repository Configuration Files
docs.text:
Example:

/etc/yum.repos.d/example.repo

A repository file contains:

  • Repository name
  • Repository URL
  • Enabled status
  • Security settings

docs.title: Trusted Software Sources
docs.text:
Linux administrators should evaluate software sources carefully.

Good sources include:

  • Official distribution repositories
  • Vendor maintained repositories
  • Internal company repositories

Avoid:

  • Unknown download sites
  • Unmaintained repositories
  • Unsupported packages

docs.title: Repository Not Found
docs.text:
Example:

Unable to locate package

Possible causes:

  • Repository missing
  • Incorrect repository configuration
  • Package unavailable

Check:

apt update

docs.title: Repository Key Errors
docs.text:
Example:

NO_PUBKEY

Possible cause:

  • Missing signing key

Solution:

  • Install the correct trusted key
  • Verify the repository source

docs.title: Failed Repository Connection
docs.text:
Possible causes:

  • Network issues
  • Incorrect URL
  • Repository outage

Test:

ping repository-server

docs.title: Linux Command Reference
docs.text:
A quick reference guide for common Linux commands used throughout the training course.

This document is designed as a companion reference and does not replace the individual lessons.

docs.title: pwd - Print Working Directory
docs.text:
Shows your current location.

pwd

Example:

/home/james/projects

docs.title: ls - List Files
docs.text:
Displays files and directories.

Basic usage:

ls

Detailed listing:

ls -l

Show hidden files:

ls -a

Human-readable sizes:

ls -lh

Common combination:

ls -lah

docs.title: cd - Change Directory
docs.text:
Move between directories.

Go to home directory:

cd

Go to a specific directory:

cd /etc

Move up one level:

cd ..

Return to previous directory:

cd -

docs.title: mkdir - Create Directory
docs.text:
Create a directory:

mkdir directory-name

Create nested directories:

mkdir -p projects/linux/module01

docs.title: touch - Create Empty File
docs.text:
Create a file:

touch notes.txt

Create multiple files:

touch file1.txt file2.txt

docs.title: cp - Copy Files
docs.text:
Copy a file:

cp source.txt destination.txt

Copy directories:

cp -r directory backup-directory

docs.title: mv - Move or Rename
docs.text:
Move a file:

mv file.txt /tmp/

Rename a file:

mv oldname.txt newname.txt

docs.title: rm - Remove Files
docs.text:
Remove a file:

rm file.txt

Remove a directory:

rm -r directory

Force removal:

rm -rf directory

⚠️ Use rm -rf carefully.

docs.title: rmdir - Remove Empty Directory
docs.text: rmdir directory-name

docs.title: cat
docs.text:
Display file contents:

cat filename

docs.title: less
docs.text:
View large files page by page:

less logfile.txt

Useful keys:

q       Quit
space   Next page
/word   Search

docs.title: head
docs.text:
Display first lines:

head file.txt

Specify number of lines:

head -n 20 file.txt

docs.title: tail
docs.text:
Display last lines:

tail logfile.txt

Follow live changes:

tail -f logfile.log

Commonly used for log monitoring.

docs.title: find
docs.text:
Search the filesystem.

Find by name:

find /home -name "*.txt"

Find files:

find . -type f

Find directories:

find . -type d

docs.title: locate
docs.text:
Fast file searching.

locate filename

Update database:

sudo updatedb

docs.title: grep
docs.text:
Search inside files.

Example:

grep error logfile.txt

Recursive search:

grep -r "error" /var/log

docs.title: chmod
docs.text:
Change permissions.

Make a script executable:

chmod +x script.sh

Numeric permissions:

chmod 755 script.sh

docs.title: chown
docs.text:
Change ownership.

Example:

sudo chown james file.txt

Change owner and group:

sudo chown james:developers file.txt

docs.title: whoami
docs.text:
Show current user:

whoami

docs.title: who
docs.text:
Show logged-in users:

who

docs.title: id
docs.text:

id

docs.text:

sudo useradd username

docs.title: passwd
docs.text:

sudo passwd username

docs.title: groupadd
docs.text:
Create group:

sudo groupadd developers

docs.title: ps
docs.text:
Display processes:

ps

Detailed view:

ps aux

docs.title: top
docs.text:
Live process monitoring:

top

docs.title: systemctl
docs.text:

Check service:

systemctl status ssh

Start service:

sudo systemctl start service-name

Enable at boot:

sudo systemctl enable service-name

docs.title: journalctl
docs.text:
View system logs.

View logs:

journalctl

Follow live logs:

journalctl -f

View service logs:

journalctl -u ssh

ip addr

ip route
